simple: the smallest box of memory that has its own number.
analogy: one slot on the pantry shelf.
precise: the fundamental storage unit of the C++ memory model; it is at least 8 bits wide, and every byte has a unique address; sizeof(char) is 1 by definition. On the machines of this course a byte is 8 bits (MA102).
source: D1 of F2-18 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: the number of a memory box.
analogy: the number painted on a slot's edge.
precise: a value that identifies one byte of memory; the address of an object is the address of its first byte. KID101 met the word at L0 (glossary); this chapter makes it exact.
source: D1, D3 of F2-18 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: a piece of memory that holds one value of one type.
analogy: a sack of rice that occupies some neighbouring slots.
precise: a region of storage with a type, a size and a lifetime (F2-23); a variable names an object. Not the same word as "object" in "object-oriented": an int is an object too.
source: D1 of F2-18 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: asks "how many boxes does this take?".
analogy: how many slots the sack needs.
precise: an operator that yields the number of bytes in the object representation of its operand's type, as a value of type std::size_t, computed at compile time.
source: D1 of F2-18 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: the exact bytes an object is made of.
analogy: what you actually see in the slots, with no labels.
precise: the sequence of sizeof(T) unsigned char values taken up by an object of type T; the value the program sees is an interpretation of these bytes by the type.
source: D1 of F2-18 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: which end of a big number goes into the first box.
analogy: whether the sack's label is written starting at the left slot or the right slot.
precise: the order in which the bytes of a multi-byte scalar are stored at increasing addresses: little-endian stores the least significant byte at the lowest address, big-endian the most significant byte. C++20 lets a program ask with std::endian::native.
source: D1, D3 of F2-18 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: the whole range of box numbers a program may use.
analogy: the full length of the numbered shelf.
precise: the set of addresses a running program can name; on the Linux systems of this course each process has its own virtual address space, which the operating system and hardware map onto physical memory (F3, curriculum B4).
source: D3 of F2-18 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: a variable that holds the address of something else.
analogy: a note with a shelf number written on it.
precise: an object of type T* whose value is the address of an object of type T, the address one past the end of an array of T, or the null pointer value.
source: D1, D2 of F2-19 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: "where is this?"
analogy: writing a shelf's number on a new note.
precise: the unary operator & applied to an lvalue of type T yields a pointer of type T* to that object. Not the same symbol use as the reference declarator T& (F2-12).
source: D1 of F2-19 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: "go to that place and use what is there."
analogy: walking to the shelf on the note.
precise: the unary * applied to a pointer yields the object it points to (an lvalue); p->m means (*p).m. Dereferencing a pointer that does not point to a live object is undefined behaviour.
source: D1 of F2-19 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: a pointer that deliberately points to nothing.
analogy: a blank note.
precise: the null pointer value of a pointer type, compares unequal to the address of every object; nullptr is the literal that converts to it. Dereferencing it is undefined behaviour.
source: D1 of F2-19 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: moving a pointer forward or back by whole elements.
analogy: "four sacks further along the shelf".
precise: adding an integer n to a pointer into an array gives a pointer n elements further; subtracting two pointers into the same array gives the number of elements between them (type std::ptrdiff_t); results outside the array, except one past its end, are undefined.
source: D1 of F2-19 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: a pointer just after the last element, used as a finish line.
analogy: the line painted after the last slot of your section.
precise: for an array of N elements, &a[0] + N; it may be computed and compared but not dereferenced. Standard iterators' end() follows the same rule (F2-15).
source: D1 of F2-19 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: a pointer to something that is gone.
analogy: a note for a shelf that was cleared and refilled.
precise: a pointer whose value was the address of an object whose lifetime has ended; using it to access memory is undefined behaviour (F2-23).
source: D1 of F2-19 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: the rule for how long an object's memory is kept.
analogy: tray (until the task ends), lent shelf (until returned), permanent shelf (all evening).
precise: the property of an object that defines the minimum lifetime of its storage: automatic, dynamic, static or thread.
source: D1 of F2-20 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: memory for function calls that is used and freed in strict last-in, first-out order.
analogy: the pile of prep trays at a cook's station.
precise: the region of memory in which an implementation keeps the frames of active function calls; objects with automatic storage duration usually live there. The C++ standard describes automatic storage, not a "stack"; the stack is how the platforms of this course implement it.
source: D1, D3 of F2-20 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: one function call's private space on the stack.
analogy: one tray.
precise: the part of the stack used by one activation of a function: its local variables, saved registers, the return address and outgoing arguments as the ABI requires (HW202 met it at machine level, glossary).
source: D3, D5 of F2-20 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: a big pool of memory you ask for while the program runs and give back when you are done.
analogy: shelves the storeroom manager lends on request.
precise: memory for objects with dynamic storage duration, obtained by new (or by containers and smart pointers on your behalf) and released by delete; the C++ standard calls it the free store, and the C library's malloc heap usually provides it. Not the same as the "heap" data structure of algorithms courses.
source: D1, D3 of F2-20 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: memory that exists for the whole run of the program.
analogy: shelves labelled and stocked before the restaurant opens.
precise: storage for objects with static storage duration (namespace-scope variables, static locals and members); it lasts from program start (or first use, for static locals) until program end.
source: D1 of F2-20 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: running out of stack, usually by calling too deep.
analogy: trays piled to the ceiling.
precise: an attempt to grow the stack beyond its reserved size; on Linux this touches an unmapped guard region and the process receives SIGSEGV, which AddressSanitizer reports as "stack-overflow".
source: D3, D6 of F2-20 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: using a local variable after its block has ended.
analogy: reaching for a tray that was already cleared.
precise: accessing an object with automatic storage duration through a pointer or reference after the block that declared it has exited; undefined behaviour, reported by AddressSanitizer as "stack-use-after-scope".
source: D1, D6 of F2-20 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: "make me an object on the heap and give me its address."
analogy: asking the storeroom manager for a shelf and stocking it.
precise: an expression that obtains storage by calling an allocation function (operator new) and then constructs an object (or array of objects) in it; it yields a pointer to the object. If allocation fails it throws std::bad_alloc (in the default form).
source: D1 of F2-21 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: "destroy this heap object and give its memory back."
analogy: clearing the shelf and handing it back.
precise: an expression that runs the destructor of the object a pointer points to and then calls a deallocation function (operator delete) to release the storage; delete[] does the same for an array created by new[]. Deleting a null pointer does nothing.
source: D1 of F2-21 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: heap memory that is never given back.
analogy: a shelf nobody returns.
precise: dynamically allocated storage that the program no longer references and never deallocates; it stays reserved until the process ends. LeakSanitizer reports it at exit.
source: D3, D6 of F2-21 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: giving the same memory back twice.
analogy: returning the same shelf twice, so it can be lent to two cooks.
precise: calling delete (or free) a second time on a pointer whose storage was already deallocated; undefined behaviour that can corrupt the allocator's data structures.
source: D1, D3 of F2-21 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: using heap memory after giving it back.
analogy: still putting flour on a shelf you returned.
precise: accessing an object through a pointer after the object was deleted; undefined behaviour, a special case of a dangling pointer (F2-19, F2-23).
source: D1 of F2-21 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: being the one responsible for giving something back.
analogy: the owner's tag on a borrowed shelf.
precise: the responsibility for ending an object's lifetime and releasing its resources; in modern C++ it is expressed by an owner object (a container, a smart pointer, an RAII handle) rather than by a raw pointer.
source: D4 of F2-21 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: an object that holds a pointer and deletes the object for you at the right time.
analogy: the shelf with an owner's tag that is returned automatically.
precise: a class template, such as std::unique_ptr or std::shared_ptr, that owns a dynamically allocated object and releases it in its destructor (RAII, F2-11). F2-22 covers them in detail.
source: D1, D2 of F2-21 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: a checker that lists, at the end of the run, memory that was never given back.
analogy: a closing-time inspection of the storeroom.
precise: a run-time leak detector that is part of AddressSanitizer on Linux; at process exit it scans memory for heap blocks no longer referenced and prints where each was allocated.
source: D6 of F2-21 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: a pointer that is the one and only owner of its object.
analogy: a borrowed tool with exactly one name tag.
precise: a class template in <memory> that owns an object through a pointer and deletes it when the unique_ptr is destroyed or reset; it can be moved (transferring ownership) but not copied.
source: D1, D2 of F2-22 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: "make one on the heap, already owned."
analogy: taking a tool and hanging your tag in one movement.
precise: a function template that constructs a T with new and returns a std::unique_ptr<T> owning it, so no raw new appears in your code.
source: D1, D4 of F2-22 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: a pointer that shares ownership with others; the object goes away when the last one lets go.
analogy: the sign-out sheet on a shared binder.
precise: a class template that shares ownership of an object through a control block holding a use count; copying increments the count, destroying or resetting decrements it, and the object is destroyed when the count reaches zero.
source: D1 of F2-22 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: the number of current owners.
analogy: the number of names not yet crossed out.
precise: the number of shared_ptr instances that share ownership of an object, reported by use_count(); it is kept in the control block and updated atomically so that copies in different threads are safe.
source: D1 of F2-22 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: a pointer that can check whether a shared object still exists, without keeping it alive.
analogy: reading the sign-out sheet without signing it.
precise: a class template that refers to an object managed by shared_ptr without contributing to its use count; lock() returns a shared_ptr that is empty if the object has already been destroyed, and expired() tells whether it has.
source: D1 of F2-22 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: two or more objects that keep each other alive, so none is ever freed.
analogy: Ana and Bo, each waiting for the other to leave.
precise: a cycle of shared_ptr references among objects; after the last outside owner is gone, every use count in the cycle stays above zero, so the objects leak. Break it with a weak_ptr on one side.
source: D1, D4 of F2-22 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: a chain of nodes where each node knows the next one.
analogy: order tickets clipped together, each clip holding the next ticket.
precise: a sequence container made of separately allocated nodes, each holding an element and a link to the next node (and in a doubly linked list, the previous one); insertion at a known position is constant time, access by index is linear.
source: D3 of F2-22 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: the time during which an object really exists and may be used.
analogy: from stocking a shelf until it is cleared.
precise: a run-time property of an object: for a class type with a non-trivial constructor it begins when initialisation completes, and it ends when the destructor call starts (or when the storage is released or reused); outside its lifetime, an object may not be accessed through its type.
source: D1 of F2-23 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: an unnamed object the compiler creates in the middle of an expression.
analogy: a plate passed through the hatch and taken back at once.
precise: an object created, for example, by a function returning by value; it is destroyed at the end of the full-expression that created it, unless it is bound to a reference that extends its lifetime.
source: D1 of F2-23 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: something the language rules do not allow, so the result can be anything.
analogy: an order the rule book has no page for.
precise: behaviour for which the C++ standard imposes no requirements; an implementation may do anything, including appearing to work, and compilers may optimise on the assumption that it does not occur. Not the same as unspecified behaviour (one of several allowed results) or implementation-defined behaviour (documented by the implementation).
source: D1 of F2-23 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: a reference, string_view or span that looks at something that no longer exists.
analogy: a window looking onto a cleared shelf.
precise: a reference or non-owning view whose referent's lifetime has ended; any access through it is undefined behaviour. std::string_view and std::span never own the data they view.
source: D1, D4 of F2-23 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: a calculation with signed integers whose true result does not fit in the type.
analogy: a counter on the wall that has no digit left.
precise: an arithmetic result outside the range of a signed integer type; undefined behaviour in C++ (unsigned arithmetic, in contrast, is defined to wrap modulo 2N; MA102).
source: D1 of F2-23 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: a checker that reports some kinds of undefined behaviour while the program runs.
analogy: an inspector who knows several pages that are missing from the rule book.
precise: compiler instrumentation enabled with -fsanitize=undefined that adds run-time checks for, among others, signed overflow, misaligned access, null member access and out-of-bounds array indexes, and prints "runtime error:" messages; by default it reports and continues.
source: D5, D6 of F2-23 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: a bug whose symptoms change or disappear when you try to look at it.
analogy: the trouble that moves to closing time when one extra note is added.
precise: informal engineering term for a defect whose observable effect depends on timing, memory layout, optimisation level or instrumentation; memory-safety bugs are a classic source because their effect depends on what else occupies the memory.
source: D3 of F2-23 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: the rule that an object of some type must start at an address that is a multiple of a certain number.
analogy: crates may start only at slots that are a multiple of 8.
precise: an implementation-defined power of two, given by alignof(T), such that every object of type T has an address that is a multiple of it; on the x86-64 build used here alignof(int) was 4 and alignof(double) 8.
source: D1, R1 of F2-24 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: unused bytes the compiler puts inside or at the end of a struct.
analogy: empty slots left so the next crate lines up.
precise: bytes of an object's representation that belong to no member; inserted so that each member meets its alignment and so that the size is a multiple of the struct's alignment (making arrays work); their values are unspecified unless the object was zero-initialised in a way that sets them.
source: D1, D3 of F2-24 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: the operator that tells you a type's alignment.
analogy: reading the "starts every N slots" label on a crate.
precise: alignof(T) yields a std::size_t constant, the alignment requirement of T; alignas requests a stricter one.
source: D1 of F2-24 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: a macro that tells you at which byte a member starts inside its struct.
analogy: "the rice starts at slot 20 of the kit".
precise: offsetof(type, member) from <cstddef>, a constant of type std::size_t; conditionally supported for types that are not standard-layout.
source: D1 of F2-24 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: a struct simple enough that its layout follows the C rules.
analogy: a kit packed by the published packing rules, without hidden extras.
precise: a class type with, among other conditions, all non-static data members having the same access control, no virtual functions or virtual base classes, and members that are themselves standard-layout; tested with std::is_standard_layout_v.
source: D1 of F2-24 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: a type whose objects may be copied by copying their bytes.
analogy: a kit you can duplicate by photocopying the shelf.
precise: a type whose copy and move operations and destructor are trivial (or deleted, with at least one eligible); for such types, copying the bytes with std::memcpy into another object of the type gives that object the same value. Tested with std::is_trivially_copyable_v.
source: D1 of F2-24 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: the rule that you may read an object only as its own type (or as raw bytes).
analogy: a flour crate must be opened as a flour crate, not as a box of rice.
precise: accessing an object through a glvalue of a type other than its dynamic type, a corresponding signed/unsigned type, or char/unsigned char/std::byte is undefined behaviour.
source: D1 of F2-24 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: turning an object into a sequence of bytes in an agreed format, and back.
analogy: writing the kit's contents onto a delivery slip in an agreed order, instead of shipping the shelf.
precise: encoding of values into a defined external representation (field order, sizes, byte order, no padding) independent of the in-memory object representation; decoding is the reverse.
source: D3 of F2-24 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: a fixed number of same-type values stored next to each other, written int a[4].
analogy: a run of numbered slots with no fence at the end.
precise: an object of type T[N] holding N contiguous elements; N is part of the type and sizeof gives N * sizeof(T); not assignable or copyable as a whole, and converted to a pointer to its first element in most expressions.
source: D1 of F2-25 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: an array turning into a pointer to its first element, losing its length.
analogy: handing over a note with the first slot number but no count.
precise: the standard conversion from an lvalue of type T[N] to a prvalue of type T*; also, a function parameter declared with array type is adjusted to pointer type.
source: D1 of F2-25 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: a fixed-size array that behaves like a normal value.
analogy: the same slots, sold as a boxed set with the count printed on the lid.
precise: the class template std::array<T, N> from <array>, an aggregate wrapping T[N], copyable and assignable, with size(), iterators, operator[] (unchecked) and at() (checked).
source: D1 of F2-25 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: a view of a run of elements that knows where it starts and how many there are.
analogy: a note with a first slot number AND a count.
precise: the class template std::span<T, Extent> from <span> (C++20), a non-owning reference to a contiguous sequence, holding a pointer and (for dynamic extent) a size; constructible from built-in arrays, std::array, std::vector and other contiguous ranges.
source: D1, D4 of F2-25 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: a test that an index is inside the array before using it.
analogy: a fence at the last slot.
precise: a run-time comparison of an index against the size, as done by at() (which throws std::out_of_range), by hardened library modes, or by sanitizer instrumentation; built-in subscripting and operator[] of standard containers do not check.
source: D1 of F2-25 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: reading or writing past the end (or before the start) of an array.
analogy: counting the coffee shelf's slot as a tip slot.
precise: an access outside the bounds of an array object; undefined behaviour in C++; reported by AddressSanitizer as stack-buffer-overflow, heap-buffer-overflow or global-buffer-overflow according to where the array lives.
source: D6 of F2-25 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: a loop or calculation that goes one step too far or stops one step short.
analogy: "while the slot number is at most four".
precise: informal term for a boundary error, typically <= where < was needed, or a size used as a last index.
source: D3 of F2-25 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: an allocator that hands out memory from one block by moving a cursor forward, and frees everything at once.
analogy: handing out counter space from left to right and wiping the whole counter at closing.
precise: a region-based allocator whose state is a base, a size and an offset; allocation rounds the offset up to the requested alignment and advances it; individual deallocation is not supported, only reset.
source: D3, S1 of F2-25 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: a list of the free pieces of a memory region, used to find room for a request and to take pieces back.
analogy: a board listing which counter sections are free right now.
precise: an allocator data structure linking free blocks (often through headers stored inside the blocks themselves); allocation searches it (first fit, best fit), may split a block; freeing returns a block and may coalesce it with free neighbours.
source: D3 of F2-25 (R = lab run in this build; D = standard, book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1; S = Systems Curriculum)

simple: a checker built into the compiler that stops a program the moment it touches memory it must not touch, and says where.
analogy: an inspector who has marked every shelf slot that is not yours and shouts as soon as you reach for one.
precise: compiler instrumentation enabled with -fsanitize=address: every load and store is checked against shadow memory that records which bytes are addressable; red zones around objects and a quarantine for freed heap blocks let it report buffer overflows, use after free, use after scope and double free with stack traces of the access, the free and the allocation. It only sees accesses that actually execute.
source: D6 of F2-21 and F2-23 (sanitizer documentation, title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1); R-records of the F2-18 to F2-25 lab runs (reports produced in this build)
